body_en:
This article is based on the Global Times video channel “Xia Baihua” video “After the Republicans' Big Defeat, Japan's Internet Did Something Absurd!” (November 6, 2026). Video link: https://weixin.qq.com/sph/ArzaFIDerz

On November 3 local time, the U.S. midterm elections ended in a crushing defeat for the Republicans. Overseas, Japan was one of the countries that reacted most intensely. Not only did Japanese officials worry about damage to their geopolitical interests — some Japanese far-right accounts went on social media to viciously attack minority candidates who had just won, even shouting: “Yesterday Europe, today America, tomorrow Japan.”

Because the social platforms involved all have auto-translate features, these extremist remarks have already drawn the attention of internet users in the U.S. and other countries.

According to reports from Reuters and Japan's Jiji Press, the Japanese government's current concern is that President Trump, having lost control of the domestic political agenda, may turn more of his energy toward foreign affairs — which could harm Japan's interests.

Japanese officials told these outlets that if Trump, seeking to build a “political legacy” for the final two years of his term, moves to further improve relations with Russia, North Korea, and other countries, Japan could be left out of the diplomatic agenda and marginalized in East Asian geopolitics.

Meanwhile, Japanese online far-right populist accounts fell into a different kind of frenzy. They claimed that “foreign immigrants” had taken over the United States, and that the election result proved it. These accounts warned that unless Japan adopted a “Japanese First” policy, it would follow in the footsteps of the U.S. and Europe and fall into the hands of “foreigners.”

To support this absurd anxiety, these far-right populist accounts deliberately clipped footage of minority American candidates celebrating their victories with voters, and attacked it with strongly racist and xenophobic language. The posts have already earned plenty of likes from other far-right populist accounts.

Here is what Japanese far-right accounts posted on X. First, this one: a Japanese account reposted footage of Democratic supporters celebrating a win, with the caption:

“Democratic Party supporters are rejoicing. America, let me ask you one thing. Isn't this despair? I'm Japanese, but I'm truly saddened.”

(Original English from X's auto-translation: Democratic Party supporters are rejoicing. America, let me ask you one thing. Isn't this despair? I'm Japanese, but I'm truly saddened.)

Then this post from Michigan. The image shows Abdul El-Sayed, the first Muslim senator, giving his victory speech. The Japanese caption reads:

“U.S. 🇺🇸 midterms, Michigan. Abdul El-Sayed, the first Muslim elected to the Senate. It would be terrible if Japan got a lawmaker like this. If the Democrats win, the world will fall into chaos again.”

(Original Japanese: アメリカ🇺🇸中間選挙、ミシガン州。イスラム教徒で初の上院議員となったアブドゥル・エルサイード。日本もこんな議員が誕生したら最悪だぞ。民主党が勝ったらまた世界がメチャクチャになるよ。)

And this one, which draws a straight line between the U.S. and Sweden:

“In the end, the U.S. midterms are just like Sweden. They let in too many immigrants, and as a result, politicians who support immigration get elected. I'm truly sick of this trend. Just thinking about the Democrats' miserable America coming back — praising LGBT people, idiotic environmental regulations, more illegal immigration — makes me depressed. In the end, Japan will be heavily affected too.”

(Original Japanese: 結局、米中間選挙もスウェーデンと同じか。移民を入れ過ぎた結果、移民を肯定する政治家が当選する。もうほんとこの流れに辟易する。また民主党のLGBT賞賛、アホ環境規制、不法移民増加の悲惨なアメリカが戻ってくると思うと憂鬱になるわ。結局それは日本も多大な影響を受けるからな。)

In fact, Japan's far-right populist forces have in recent years been actively learning from America's far-right populists. According to the Associated Press and Asahi Shimbun, Japan's far-right party Sanseito has not only copied the American anti-immigration, anti-diversity political playbook wholesale — exaggerating the threat foreigners pose to Japan and promoting a Japanese-first ideology — it also invited Charlie Kirk, the leading figure of American far-right populism who was assassinated last year, to speak in Japan and share his experience.

And since Sanae Takaichi became Japan's prime minister last year, her deliberate courting of the domestic far-right populist camp has given its highly controversial demands an even bigger stage. At the same time, her fawning deference to the U.S. government has further deepened the ties between the Japanese and American far-right populist movements. So when the Republicans lost the midterms, the Japanese far right's mindset collapsed right along with them.

Most of these Japanese far-right populist accounts post on X. Thanks to the platform's auto-translate feature, their xenophobic posts were automatically rendered into English and other languages and pushed by the algorithm to users in the U.S. and beyond — letting the whole world get a direct look at the online ecosystem of Japan under Takaichi.
excerpt_en: When Republicans lost the 2026 U.S. midterms, Japan reacted more intensely than almost anywhere — its government fretted about being sidelined, while far-right accounts attacked minority candidates who had just won.
title_en: After the Republicans' Big Defeat, Japan's Internet Did Something Absurd
